States of Christ (Humiliation and Exaltation)
STAYTS of KRAIST
noun phrase (Christology)
The Reformed-confessional doctrine of the two states of the Mediator: the state of humiliation (Christ's condescension in His incarnation, suffering, death, and burial) and the state of exaltation (His resurrection, ascension, session at the Father's right hand, and return in glory). Westminster Shorter Catechism Q. 27-28; Larger Catechism Q. 46-56.

📖 Biblical Definition

The Reformed-confessional doctrine of the two states of the Mediator: the state of humiliation and the state of exaltation, describing the two great phases of Christ's mediatorial work. The doctrine is grounded principally in Philippians 2:5-11 (the Christ-hymn, descending into humiliation and ascending into exaltation) and codified in the Reformed confessions (Westminster Shorter Catechism Q. 27-28; Larger Catechism Q. 46-56). The state of humiliation comprises Christ's condescension and the lowliness He endured for our salvation: His incarnation (taking our nature, born in a low condition); His subjection to the law; His enduring the miseries of this life, the wrath of God, and the cursed death of the cross; His being buried and continuing under the power of death for a time (Westminster Shorter Catechism Q. 27, Christ's humiliation consisted in his being born, and that in a low condition, made under the law, undergoing the miseries of this life, the wrath of God, and the cursed death of the cross; in being buried, and continuing under the power of death for a time). The state of exaltation comprises Christ's glorification: His resurrection from the dead on the third day; His ascension into heaven; His sitting at the right hand of God the Father; and His coming to judge the world at the last day (Westminster Shorter Catechism Q. 28, Christ's exaltation consisteth in his rising again from the dead on the third day, in ascending up into heaven, in sitting at the right hand of God the Father, and in coming to judge the world at the last day). The two states correspond to the descent and ascent of Philippians 2: the eternal Son descended into the depths of humiliation (emptying Himself, taking the form of a servant, humbling Himself unto death, even the death of the cross) and was then exalted to the heights (God highly exalted Him and gave Him a name above every name). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine of the two states as a comprehensive framework for the mediatorial work of Christ: the humiliation by which He accomplished redemption (descending to bear our guilt and curse) and the exaltation by which He was vindicated and now reigns (ascending to His glory and rule); the believer's salvation rests on both — redeemed by the humiliation, and saved to the uttermost by the living, reigning, interceding, returning, exalted Christ.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The Reformed-confessional doctrine of the two states of the Mediator: humiliation (incarnation, subjection to the law, suffering, the cursed death of the cross, burial, continuing under death) and exaltation (resurrection, ascension, session at the Father's right hand, return in glory); grounded in Philippians 2:5-11; Westminster Shorter Catechism Q. 27-28.

STATES OF CHRIST (HUMILIATION AND EXALTATION), n. phr. (Christology) The two states of the Mediator. Grounded in Philippians 2:5-11; Westminster Shorter Catechism Q. 27-28; Larger Catechism Q. 46-56. Humiliation (Q. 27): being born in a low condition, made under the law, undergoing the miseries of this life, the wrath of God, and the cursed death of the cross; being buried and continuing under the power of death for a time. Exaltation (Q. 28): rising again on the third day, ascending into heaven, sitting at the right hand of God the Father, and coming to judge the world at the last day. The descent and ascent of Philippians 2: the Son descended into humiliation (emptying Himself, the form of a servant, obedient unto death) and was exalted to the heights (a name above every name).

📖 Key Scripture

Philippians 2:8-9 — "And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name."

Luke 24:26 — "Ought not Christ to have suffered these things, and to enter into his glory?"

Ephesians 1:20-21 — "Which he wrought in Christ, when he raised him from the dead, and set him at his own right hand in the heavenly places, Far above all principality, and power, and might, and dominion."

1 Peter 1:11 — "Searching what, or what manner of time the Spirit of Christ which was in them did signify, when it testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ, and the glory that should follow."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The two states of Christ are the comprehensive framework for His mediatorial work; the principal mishandling is the neglect of one state — emphasizing the humiliation (the suffering Savior) while neglecting the exaltation (the reigning Lord), or vice versa.

expand to see more

States of Christ as a doctrine does not undergo lexical corruption. The principal mishandling is the neglect of one state at the expense of the other. Some traditions and spiritualities emphasize the humiliation of Christ (the suffering Savior, the crucified Christ, the man of sorrows) while neglecting the exaltation (the risen, ascended, reigning, returning Lord); this can produce a Christianity fixated on the cross and the suffering Christ without the triumphant note of the resurrection, ascension, and reign. Others emphasize the exaltation (the glorious reigning Christ, the triumphant King) while neglecting the humiliation (the depths of suffering by which He accomplished redemption); this can produce a triumphalism that loses sight of the cross. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine of the two states in their fulness: the humiliation by which Christ accomplished redemption (descending to bear our guilt, endure the wrath of God, die the cursed death of the cross, and continue under death's power for a time) and the exaltation by which He was vindicated and now reigns (rising from the dead, ascending to heaven, sitting at the Father's right hand, and returning to judge the world). Both states are essential to the gospel and to the believer's salvation: he is redeemed by the humiliation of Christ (the crucified Savior who bore his sins) and saved to the uttermost by the exaltation of Christ (the living, reigning, interceding, returning Lord). Luke 24:26 holds the two together: Ought not Christ to have suffered these things, and to enter into his glory? — the suffering (humiliation) and the glory (exaltation) are the two great phases of the one mediatorial work.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The two states of the Mediator: humiliation (incarnation, suffering, the cross, burial) and exaltation (resurrection, ascension, session, return); Philippians 2:5-11; Westminster Shorter Catechism Q. 27-28.
